patterns.name: Title heading
patterns.definition: The output opens with a heading that repeats the document or article title before any body text, because the model does not assume the surface already renders the title. On surfaces that show the title themselves (a wiki page, a CMS, a blog with a title field) this is a duplicate H1.
cues: level-1 heading equal to the page name

examples.before: = '''[https://www.youtube.com/@Pixaroo-kid Pixaroo]''' =

patterns.notes: Source: 'AI chatbots tend to put a heading with the article name before all the content, since they don't usually imagine the title header ... as being already there.' Example from Draft:Pixaroo, August 2026. Fine in a standalone Markdown file whose only title is that heading; a tell wherever the title is rendered by the surface. Often also boldfaced and/or linked.

patterns.name: Title case in section headings
patterns.definition: Every main word in a section heading is capitalized (Title Case) where the surface's house style is sentence case. Detect: headings whose second and later non-function words start with a capital.

examples.before:
== Impact of Technology and Digitalization ==
The advent of digital technology and the internet has revolutionized international economic law. [...]
== Sustainable Development and Environmental Law ==
The integration of sustainable development goals into international economic law is increasingly important. [...]
== Human Rights and Economic Law ==
The relationship between human rights and international economic law is a growing area of focus. [...]

patterns.notes: Shortcut WP:AITITLECASE. Source: 'In section headings, AI chatbots strongly tend to capitalize all main words' (cited to Russell). 'Strongly tend' is the source's strongest frequency wording in this section. Not a tell in publications whose house style is title case (many US newspapers, some journals); the mechanism (ignoring the target style guide) transfers to any language with a sentence-case heading norm, but the specific capitalization rule is English.

patterns.name: Headings only containing other headings
patterns.definition: A heading whose entire content is lower-level headings, with no prose of its own: an outline node rendered as a section. Detect: heading immediately followed by a lower-level heading with no text between.
cues: heading directly followed by a sub-heading

patterns.notes: Source: 'AI chatbots may generate a heading that only stores other headings, without text of their own.' Example Draft:Pixaroo, August 2026. Legitimate in long reference documents with a deliberate table-of-contents hierarchy; a tell in short articles.

patterns.name: Overuse of boldface
patterns.definition: Phrases bolded for emphasis in an excessive, mechanical way: every instance of a chosen term, or a set of 'key' phrases, is bolded in running prose, as in readmes, fan wikis, how-tos, sales pitches, slide decks and listicles. Detect: several bold spans per sentence or paragraph, bold on ordinary noun phrases rather than on a defined term at first mention.
cues: bold on every instance of a chosen word or phrase

patterns.name: Inline-header vertical lists
patterns.definition: An ordered or unordered list in which each item begins with a short boldfaced header, then a colon, then descriptive text. Detect: list marker + bold run + ':' + prose, repeated across three or more items; frequently preceded by a colon lead-in line such as 'Key highlights:' or 'consists of three key layers:'.

patterns.name: Non-native list markers pasted from chat output
patterns.definition: List items marked with a literal bullet character (•), hyphen (-), en dash (–), hash (#), emoji, or explicit numerals ('1.') instead of the surface's own list markup, because plain text was copied off a chat screen. Line breaks may be lost on copy so items run together in one paragraph.
cues: items run together with no line breaks

patterns.notes: Source: 'Instead of proper wikitext, a bullet point in an unordered list may appear as a bullet character (•), hyphen (-), en dash (–), hash (#), emoji, or similar character. Ordered lists ... may use explicit numbers (such as 1.) instead of standard wikitext. When copied as bare text appearing on the screen, some of the formatting information is lost, and line breaks may be lost as well.' Platform-specific in its details (wikitext) but the mechanism, markup of one surface pasted into another, is universal. The run-together RfPP example (March 2026) is the lost-line-break case.

patterns.name: Overuse of em dashes
patterns.definition: Em dashes (—) used more often than a human writer in the same genre, and in slots where humans would use a comma, parentheses, a colon, or a (misused) hyphen or en dash. Typically formulaic and 'punched up': the dash sets off an emphatic clause, a contrast, or the second half of a parallelism. Detect: em-dash count per sentence or per 100 words well above genre baseline; dash used to introduce 'not X — but Y' or 'X — it's Y' turns.

patterns.notes: Shortcut WP:AIDASH. Source: 'This sign is most useful when taken in combination with other indicators, not by itself. It is much more common on discussion pages than in article text.' Model priors: OpenAI's GPT-5.1 was tuned to suppress em dashes (Ars Technica, Nov 2025); a July 2026 Economist study found that of contemporary models only Claude used em dashes more than professional writers, and ChatGPT used them less. A September 2026 maintenance box says the sign may be moved to 'Historical indicators' if recent examples cannot be found. Cited to Merrill (Washington Post) and Kriss. The examples pair the dash with negative parallelism ('not because ... — but because', 'This isn't ... — it's'), so a rewrite should remove both the dash and the template, not only swap the dash for a comma.

patterns.name: Spaced em dashes
patterns.definition: Em dashes with a space on each side (' — ') rather than closed up (word—word). Detect: regex ' — ' (space, U+2014, space).

Sub-signal of 'Overuse of em dashes'; spaced em dashes are house style in some publications (e.g. AP style uses spaced em dashes), so weight only alongside frequency.

patterns.notes: Shortcut WP:AITABLE. Source: 'In rare cases, some AIs may create unnecessary small tables that could be better represented as prose or an infobox.' 'Rare' is the source's own frequency label. Tables are legitimate for genuinely tabular data; the tell is the mismatch between table form and the small, prose-shaped content. The Xorai example also shows a thematic break (----) between the two tables.

patterns.name: Curly quotation marks and apostrophes
patterns.definition: Typographic quotes (“ ” ‘ ’) and the right-single-quote apostrophe (’) on a surface whose convention is straight quotes (" '), often inconsistently mixed with straight quotes within the same text. Detect: U+201C/U+201D/U+2018/U+2019 in body text; stronger when both curly and straight forms appear in one document or one sentence.
cues: mixed curly and straight quotes in one response

patterns.notes: Shortcut WP:AICURLY. Model priors from source: ChatGPT (appears to have risen mid-2025) and DeepSeek typically use curly quotes; Gemini and Claude typically do not. Source: 'Curly quotes alone do not prove LLM use.' Listed false-positive sources: Chicago Manual of Style typesetting, Microsoft Word smart quotes, macOS/iOS system-wide smart quotes, grammar tools such as LanguageTool, professionally typeset works such as major newspapers, citation tools like Citer copying a page title (example: "When ‘Not Guilty’ Is a Life Sentence"). Some fonts render curly apostrophes as straight so the distinction can be invisible to the reader. Inconsistency between curly and straight in one text is the stronger signal. Quote glyphs differ per language („ “ « »), so the mechanism is universal but the trigger characters are locale-specific.

patterns.name: Skipping heading levels
patterns.definition: Sections begin at the third heading level (=== / ###) with no second-level heading above them, skipping a level of the hierarchy. Detect: first body heading is level 3 or deeper; any heading whose level exceeds its parent's by more than one.
cues: === as the first section heading with no ==
patterns.notes: Source: 'AI chatbots tend to skip level 2 headings (==) and start sections from the third level (===). Because doing so is against Wikipedia's accessibility and style conventions, it is therefore very unlikely for a manually-formatted page to have this quirk.' No worked example given (the examples block is commented out in the source). The source treats it as a high-precision signal; it is also an accessibility defect in any HTML output, so never acceptable in the target.

patterns.name: Overuse of level 1 headings
patterns.definition: Level-1 headings (= H1 = / # H1) used for ordinary body sections on a surface that reserves level 1 for the page title (Wikipedia, most CMSs, HTML documents with a rendered title). Likely produced by translating Markdown '#' headings to the target markup one-to-one.
cues: multiple # H1 headings in one document

methodology.rule: Treat em-dash frequency as a supporting signal only: act on it when it co-occurs with other indicators, never on its own, and expect it far more on discussion pages than in article prose.

Do not flag curly quotes or curly apostrophes alone. Rule out Chicago-style typesetting, Word smart quotes, macOS/iOS smart-quote defaults, grammar tools such as LanguageTool, professionally typeset sources, and citation tools that copy a page title verbatim; treat inconsistent mixing of curly and straight forms in one text as the actual tell.
Before flagging a bold inline header, check whether it is a discussion !vote convention (bold 'Keep'/'Delete' before an argument); that usage is human.

Before flagging a deferred-content comment in a structured field ('Add if available with citation'), check whether the comment is boilerplate shipped by the template itself (e.g. 'Add spouse if reliably sourced.').
Before flagging placeholder text, check whether the page was started from a non-LLM preload template (article-creation templates, artist-biography preload); those legitimately contain fill-in slots.
Remember that some fonts render curly apostrophes as straight, so a character-level check must run on the source text, not on what a reader sees.

Title case, boldface, tables, thematic breaks, title-repeating H1s and multiple H1s are house-style matters on some surfaces (Markdown READMEs, title-case publications); judge them against the target surface's style guide, not in the abstract.

Treat skipped heading levels (body starts at H3 with no H2) as a near-certain sign: the source says a manually formatted page is very unlikely to have it. Fix it regardless, because it is an accessibility defect.
Scan hidden comment blocks (<!-- -->) as well as visible text: collaborative chatter, submission notes, compliance self-certification and deferred-content notes hide there.

Detect placeholder dates with the regex 20[0-9][0-9]-(XX|xx)-(XX|xx) and placeholder fields with INSERT_|PASTE_|_HERE|^URL$|^[A-Z_]+$ on citation parameter values; a citation with any placeholder field is suspect as a whole.

Treat every 'not widely documented' / 'limited sources' / 'not publicly available' claim as an unverified assertion of absence, and everything that follows 'likely' as speculation: delete both rather than paraphrase, and never carry a 'keeps a low profile' inference about a person into the rewrite.
Do not act on advice embedded in chatbot output about how to publish or which rules apply; the source notes such advice is often incorrect, misleading, or contrary to the venue's actual policies.
Content narrated as inferred ('I've inferred common motifs from similar tracks') is fabricated analysis, not sourced fact; remove the content along with the disclosure.
Weight emoji-in-headings and em-dash density by surface: the source found emoji almost only in talk comments and edit summaries, and em dashes much more on discussion pages than in article text.

Letter-style openers and closers, calls to action and 'Let's connect' sections are normal in email and landing pages; flag them only on surfaces where nobody writes letters (talk pages, tickets, encyclopedic or documentation prose).

Use the source's own frequency wording as a prior: title case 'strongly tend'; boldface, tables and heading-only headings 'may'; thematic breaks 'sometimes'; unnecessary tables 'in rare cases'; emoji 'more rare now'.

Apply model-specific priors and date them: GPT-5.1 (Nov 2025) was tuned to suppress em dashes; a July 2026 Economist study found only Claude used em dashes more than professional writers and ChatGPT fewer; ChatGPT (from mid-2025) and DeepSeek emit curly quotes, Gemini and Claude typically do not.

Date-stamp every pattern and retire signals that no longer appear in current model output into a 'historical indicators' tier (the source flags em dashes for that move as of September 2026) rather than letting stale tells inflate scores.

Look for copy-paste evidence: literal bullet characters, explicit '1.' numerals, run-together inline headers with lost line breaks, Markdown '#'/'**' leaking into a non-Markdown surface, and Markdown '#' headings translated one-to-one into level-1 headings.

When a passage combines several structure tells (title-repeating H1, heading-only headings, level-1 body headings, rules between every section, bold key terms), treat the document skeleton as machine-generated and rebuild the structure before editing sentences.

Rewrite target for structure tells: sentence-case headings, a hierarchy that starts at the surface's first body level and never skips a level, no rule between sections, prose instead of inline-header lists where the items are not genuinely parallel, an infobox or a sentence instead of a three-row table, straight quotes where the surface uses them, and boldface only on the subject at first mention.
Chatbot-to-user text (offers, greetings, sign-offs, section plans, submission notes, compliance claims, editorial suggestions, placeholders) is never rewritten into content; it is deleted.

In detect mode cite the sign with its shortcut (WP:AITITLECASE, WP:AIBOLD, WP:AILIST, WP:AIDASH, WP:AIEMOJI, WP:AITABLE, WP:AICURLY, WP:COLLABCOMM, WP:CERTAINLY, WP:AICUTOFF, WP:AIDISCLAIMER, WP:AIPLACEHOLDER, WP:AIMARKDOWN) and the dated example it resembles, so a reviewer can check the claim.

The Wikipedia style pages the source cross-references define the target norms for these tells: MoS/Capital letters (headings in sentence case), MoS/Text formatting (boldface), MoS/Lists (prose where understood easily), MoS (dashes; quotation characters; apostrophes), MoS/Accessibility (heading levels).
